Country in the Southern Levant region of [[West Asia]], bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, and Egypt, with coasts on the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea. [[Jerusalem]] is the seat of government and proclaimed capital, though its status receives limited international recognition; Tel Aviv is the largest urban area and economic center.

European antisemitism in the late 19th century galvanized [[Zionism]], which sought a Jewish homeland in Palestine and gained British support with the Balfour Declaration. After World War I, Britain established [[Mandatory Palestine]] in 1920. Civil war between Jews and the Arab-majority population followed the UN partition proposal of 1947. Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, and neighboring Arab states invaded the next day. Most Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled in what Palestinians call the [[Nakba]]. After the [[Six-Day War]] of 1967, Israel occupied the West Bank, Gaza, and Sinai, and annexed East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Peace treaties followed with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994). The 1993 [[Oslo Accords]] introduced limited Palestinian self-rule, and the 2020 Abraham Accords normalized ties with more Arab states, but the Israeli–Palestinian conflict persists. Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories has drawn international criticism, and many Middle East experts describe its treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank as apartheid. After the Hamas-led [[October 7 attacks]], Israel's campaign in Gaza prompted accusations of genocide, which Israel and its allies, including the U.S., deny.

The Knesset is a proportionally elected parliament; the prime minister leads the government, and the president is largely ceremonial. Israel has one of the Middle East's largest economies, ranks 12th in nominal GDP per capita, devotes a larger share of its economy to research and development than any other state, and is believed to possess nuclear weapons.

Largest city (pop. over 15 million) of Turkey, a transcontinental megacity on the Bosphorus and its economic, cultural, and historical center. Formerly Constantinople, it lies in northwestern Turkey between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea; about two-thirds of its people live in Europe and the rest in Asia. It holds 18% of Turkey's population and accounts for about 30% of the country's economy.

Neolithic artifacts indicate that the historic peninsula was settled as far back as the 6th millennium BC. Greek colonists, led according to tradition by Byzas, founded Byzantium in the seventh century BC, around 657 BC. The Roman emperor [[Constantine the Great]] refounded it as Constantinople in AD 330. For nearly 16 centuries it was the capital of four empires: the Roman Empire (330–395), the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire (395–1204 and 1261–1453), the Latin Empire (1204–1261), and the Ottoman Empire (1453–1922). It was instrumental in the advancement of Christianity in Roman and Byzantine times. [[Mehmed II]] captured it on May 29, 1453, after a 53-day siege, and the Ottomans made it the seat of their caliphate. The Republic of Turkey established its capital in Ankara in 1923, and Istanbul became the official name in 1930.

The population has increased tenfold since the 1950s as migrants from across Anatolia arrived. Most citizens are ethnic Turks; Kurds are the largest minority. The Istanbul–İzmit area is one of Turkey's main industrial regions, and the city has two international airports, multiple ports, and numerous universities. The historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Because of its proximity to the North Anatolian Fault, the city is vulnerable to earthquakes.

Country (pop. nearly 59 million) in Southern and Western Europe, officially the Italian Republic, with Rome as its capital. It consists of a peninsula extending into the [[Mediterranean Sea]], with the [[Alps]] on its northern land border, and nearly 800 islands, notably Sicily and Sardinia. It covers 301,340 sq km and borders France, Switzerland, Austria, and Slovenia, and surrounds the enclaves of Vatican City and San Marino.

Italy's history reaches back to numerous Italic peoples, notably the ancient Romans, who conquered the Mediterranean world under the Roman Republic and ruled it for centuries under the Roman Empire. The Western Roman Empire fell between late antiquity and the Early Middle Ages. By the 11th century, Italian city-states and maritime republics expanded, bringing renewed prosperity through commerce. The Italian [[Renaissance]] flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries and spread across Europe. After centuries of political division, the Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861. Italy fought in World War I from 1915 to 1918 on the side of the Entente. A fascist dictatorship was established in 1922. In World War II Italy was first part of the Axis, then a co-belligerent of the Allies after an armistice (1940–43). In 1946 the monarchy was replaced by a republic.

Italy is a developed country with one of the world's largest economies by nominal and PPP-adjusted GDP and the second-largest manufacturing sector in Europe. It is a founding member of the [[European Union]] and of NATO. It has the highest number of World Heritage Sites (62) and is the fifth most visited country in the world by international tourist arrivals.

Indian religion, also called Jain Dharma, teaching a path to spiritual purity and liberation through disciplined nonviolence (*ahimsa*) toward all living creatures. It is guided by 24 *tirthankaras* ("ford-makers"), supreme teachers who have conquered the cycle of rebirth and attained omniscience (*kevala jnana*). Its goal is *moksha*, liberation from [[Karma|karma]].

Three principles form the core of Jain philosophy: *ahimsa*, *anekantavada* (non-absolutism, the view that reality has many aspects and no single viewpoint is complete), and *aparigraha* (non-possession). Purification of the soul is held to be achievable through the three jewels: right vision, right knowledge, and right conduct. Jainism teaches five vows: nonviolence, truth, not stealing, celibacy, and non-possession. They are called *mahavratas* (great vows) for monks and nuns, and *anuvratas* (small vows) for laypersons.

In tradition, the first *tirthankara* of the current cycle was Rishabhanatha. Historians date the 23rd, Parshvanatha, to the 8th or 7th century BCE. The 24th and last, [[Mahavira]], lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE, was a contemporary of [[The Buddha|the Buddha]], and was a central figure in the Śramaṇa movement of Greater [[Magadha]], which rejected the authority of the [[Vedas]].

Applying nonviolence, the community avoided agriculture and warfare, and many Jains became merchants and bankers in ancient and medieval [[India]]. It supported networks of temples, libraries, and charitable institutions. Jainism has between four and five million followers, mostly in India, with communities in North America, Europe, and East Asia. Two sub-traditions, the Digambaras ("sky-clad") and Śvētāmbaras ("white-clad"), differ on ascetic practices, gender, and canonical texts. Major festivals include Paryushana and [[Diwali]].

Capital and largest city (pop. 11 million registered residents) of Indonesia, officially the Special Capital Region of Jakarta, with administrative status equivalent to a province. It lies on the northwestern coast of [[Java]], facing the Java Sea, and covers about 664 sq km. Its metropolitan area, known locally as Jabodetabek, extends into Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, and Bekasi, and had a population of nearly 42 million according to the UN.

The area was long associated with Sunda Kelapa, a principal port of the Sunda Kingdom. Islamic forces captured Kalapa in 1527, after which it became known as Jayakarta, a Sanskrit-derived name meaning "victory" or "victorious deed," under the Banten Sultanate. The [[Dutch East India Company]] seized Jayakarta in 1619 and rebuilt it as Batavia, its main administrative center in Asia and an important trading port. During the Japanese occupation in World War II, the authorities renamed Batavia as Jakarta. Indonesian independence was proclaimed there in 1945, and after the [[Indonesian National Revolution]], Jakarta became the capital of the unitary republic in 1950.

The city grew rapidly after independence, and migration from across Indonesia has shaped its population and culture. It has no ethnic majority; the largest groups include Javanese, Betawi, Sundanese, and Chinese Indonesians. Jakarta is Indonesia's financial and trade center and the center of national administration, and it hosts many corporate headquarters, media organizations, and universities, as well as the secretariat of [[ASEAN]].

Persistent problems include traffic congestion, flooding, land subsidence, air pollution, and pressure on water and waste services. In 2022 the Indonesian government began the legal process of moving the capital to Nusantara in East Kalimantan. Jakarta remains the capital until the transfer is formalized by a presidential decree.

Scottish physicist and mathematician who formulated the classical theory of electromagnetic radiation, the first theory to describe electricity, magnetism, and light as different manifestations of the same phenomenon. Born in Edinburgh, he graduated from Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1854, earning distinction in mathematics and the Smith's Prize. He later held the chair of natural philosophy at Marischal College in Aberdeen, where he proposed that the rings of Saturn were composed of numerous small particles, work that earned him the Adams Prize. From 1860 to 1865 he was professor of natural philosophy at King's College London. His 1865 paper "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" showed that electric and magnetic fields travel through space as waves at the speed of light, and led to his prediction of the existence of [[Radio wave|radio waves]]. The four equations now known as [[Maxwell's equations]] appear in his 1873 *A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism* and are regarded as the second great unification in physics, after that achieved by [[Isaac Newton]].

Maxwell was the first to derive the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution]], describing the speeds of gas molecules, and was key in the creation of [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]]. In 1861 he presented the first durable color photograph, and showed that any color can be produced by mixing three primary colors: red, green, and blue. His 1863 paper "On Governors" is a foundation of [[Control theory|control theory]] and cybernetics. In 1867 he proposed the thought experiment known as [[Maxwell's demon]].

In 1871 he returned to Cambridge as the first Cavendish Professor of Physics and oversaw construction of the Cavendish Laboratory. He is regarded as a founder of modern electrical engineering, and his work laid foundations for relativity and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]].

Island country (pop. almost 123 million) in East Asia, in the Pacific Ocean off the northeast coast of the Asian mainland, with Tokyo as its capital and largest city. It is bordered by the Sea of Japan to the west, the Sea of Okhotsk to the north, and the East China Sea to the south. The archipelago has four major islands and over 14,000 smaller ones, and the country is divided into 47 prefectures.

The first known habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic, c. 36,000 BC. From the 12th century, real power was held by military aristocrats known as shōgun, enforced by the warrior nobility, the samurai. The [[Tokugawa shogunate]] unified Japan in 1600 and pursued an isolationist foreign policy until an American fleet forced the opening of trade in 1853. Imperial power was restored in 1868. In the Meiji period Japan industrialized rapidly, adopted the Meiji Constitution in 1889, and annexed Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910. It invaded China in 1937 and attacked the U.S. and European colonial powers in 1941, entering World War II as an Axis power. After the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]], it surrendered in 1945 and was under Allied occupation until 1952.

Japan experienced rapid economic growth in the following decades, but since the collapse of its asset price bubble in the early 1990s has had a prolonged stagnation known as the Lost Decades. It is a constitutional monarchy with a bicameral legislature, the National Diet, and the only Asian member of the G7. It is a leader in automotive, electronics, and robotics industries and has one of the world's highest life expectancies, but its population is declining.

Principal language of the Japonic family, with around 123 million speakers, primarily in [[Japan]], the only country where it is the national language. Proposals linking it to Ainu, Austronesian, Koreanic, and the discredited Altaic have not gained wide acceptance. Proto-Japonic is thought to have been brought from the Korean peninsula in the early to mid-4th century BC, during the Yayoi period.

Chinese documents of the 3rd century AD recorded a few Japanese words, but substantial Old Japanese texts date from the 8th century. The *Kojiki*, the earliest text, was written entirely in Chinese characters. Early Middle Japanese is the language of the Heian period (794–1185), when waves of Sino-Japanese vocabulary entered the language and made it mora-timed. Late Middle Japanese (1185–1600) saw extensive grammatical change and the first European loanwords. The basis of the standard dialect moved from the Kansai region to the Edo region (modern Tokyo) in the early modern period. After the end of Japan's isolation in 1853, loanwords from European languages increased significantly, and words from English roots have proliferated.

Japanese is agglutinative and mora-timed, with a pure vowel system, phonemic vowel and consonant length, and a lexically significant pitch accent. Word order is normally subject–object–verb, with particles marking grammatical function and sentence structure that is topic–comment. Nouns have no grammatical number or gender, and there are no articles. Verbs and adjectives are conjugated, verbs primarily for tense and voice but not person. A complex system of honorifics indicates the relative status of the speaker, the listener, and persons mentioned.

The writing system combines Chinese characters, called *kanji*, with two syllabaries derived from them, *hiragana* and *katakana*. Latin script (*rōmaji*) is used in a limited fashion, for example for imported acronyms.

Island of Indonesia, one of the Greater Sunda Islands, bordered by the Indian Ocean to the south and the Java Sea to the north. It is the world's most populous island, with about 56% of the Indonesian population on only 7% of its land area. It is the world's 13th largest island. [[Jakarta]], Indonesia's capital, lies on its northwestern coast. Java dominates Indonesia politically, economically, and culturally.

The island was formed by volcanic eruptions caused by the subduction of the Australian Plate under the Sunda Plate. A chain of volcanic mountains forms its east–west spine, and the highest, Mount Semeru, reaches 3,676 m. Mount Merapi is the most active volcano in Java and in Indonesia. The mountains split the interior into relatively isolated regions suited to wet-rice cultivation, and its rice lands are among the richest in the world. Indonesian coffee was first grown on Java, beginning in 1699. Java is divided into four provinces, Banten, West Java, Central Java, and East Java, and two special regions, Jakarta and Yogyakarta.

Four main languages are spoken: Javanese, Sundanese, Madurese, and Betawi. Javanese and Sundanese are the most widely spoken; the Javanese live in the central and eastern parts and the Sundanese in the west. The majority are Muslim, but the population includes diverse religious beliefs.

Java was the center of powerful Hindu-Buddhist empires and Islamic sultanates, and the core of the colonial [[Dutch East Indies]]. It was also the center of the Indonesian struggle for independence in the 1930s and 1940s. Five of Indonesia's ten UNESCO World Heritage Sites are on Java, among them Borobudur, Prambanan, Ujung Kulon National Park, and Yogyakarta.

Music genre that originated in the African-American communities of New Orleans, Louisiana, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its roots lie in [[Blues|blues]], [[Ragtime|ragtime]], European harmony, African rhythmic rituals, spirituals, hymns, marches, vaudeville song, and dance music. It is characterized by swing and blue notes, complex chords, call-and-response vocals, polyrhythms, and improvisation. Since the 1920s Jazz Age it has been recognized as a major form of musical expression in both traditional and popular music.

The origin of the word is much researched. It is believed to be related to *jasm*, a slang term dating to 1860 meaning "pep, energy." The earliest written record, in a 1912 *Los Angeles Times* article, concerns a baseball pitch called a "jazz ball." The American Dialect Society named it the Word of the 20th Century.

Jazz is difficult to define because it spans more than 100 years, from ragtime to rock-infused fusion. [[Duke Ellington]] said, "It's all music."

Jazz did not begin as a single tradition. New Orleans jazz began in the early 1910s, combining brass band marches, French quadrilles, biguine, ragtime, and blues with collective polyphonic improvisation. In the 1930s the prominent styles were swing big bands, Kansas City jazz, and gypsy jazz. Bebop emerged in the 1940s, moving jazz from danceable popular music to a more challenging "musician's music" played at faster tempos. The mid-1950s brought hard bop, and the late 1950s modal jazz and free jazz, which explored playing without regular meter, beat, and formal structures. Jazz fusion, combining improvisation with rock's rhythms and electric instruments, appeared in the late 1960s and early 1970s; its commercial form, smooth jazz, succeeded in the early 1980s.
